output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025 examining the relationship between tree canopy cover and July afternoon land-surface temperature (LST). After accounting for impervious surfaces and building density, each 10-percentage-point increase in canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature; the brief emphasizes that this is an association, not evidence of causation. Impervious surface was the strongest single predictor, and heat-related emergency calls were higher in the hottest quartile than in the coolest. The authors recommend prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide canopy target of 30% by 2035, while noting limitations of LST and the study design. [S1][S2][S3][S4]
output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, describes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It reports that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average July-afternoon land-surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents these findings as support for a targeted planting program in the hottest neighborhoods. [S1]

For its methods, the study measured neighborhood tree canopy from 2024 aerial imagery; coverage ranged from 6% to 41%. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors. [S2]

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C—a 6.4°C difference. Share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, followed by canopy cover. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile. [S3]

The brief cautions that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, and that its cross-sectional design demonstrates association rather than causation. It also notes that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. Its recommendations are to prioritize planting in Eastgate and Millbrook, set a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035, and consider an estimated cost of about $2.1 million over ten years for planting 6,000 street trees. [S4]

key_findings.text: Each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density.
Canopy cover across the 48 neighborhoods ranged from 6% to 41%; Eastgate averaged 41.2°C and Willow Park averaged 34.8°C, a difference of 6.4°C.
Share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, with canopy cover the second strongest.
Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile.

output.executive_summary: The Catalog Modernization Project is rated Amber: it remains on schedule for the planned November 17, 2026 go-live, but its forecast cost is $6,500 above the approved budget. Migration is 85% complete, and the quarter included completed data mapping, a pilot migration, and successful usability testing of the new search interface. Staff training is in progress, and the project is addressing risks from duplicate legacy records and the departure of the vendor’s lead migration engineer. Reported follow-up includes issuing a revised training schedule, completing a deduplication report, confirming contingency funding, and obtaining a vendor staffing transition plan. [S1][S2][S3]
output.detailed_summary:
The report covers July 1 to September 30, 2026, was prepared by Project Manager Elena Vasquez, and is dated October 6, 2026. Overall status is Amber. The project is on schedule for go-live, while over budget. Data migration is 85% complete, with 412,000 of 485,000 catalog records migrated to the new platform provided by Larkspur Data Services LLC. The planned go-live date is November 17, 2026; public access to the legacy catalog will end that same day. [S1]

During the quarter, data mapping was completed on July 24, 2026, and the pilot migration was completed at the Central branch on August 28, 2026. The new patron search interface passed usability testing with 18 volunteer patrons. The approved budget is $180,000; spending as of September 30, 2026 was $112,400, and the forecast at completion is $186,500, or $6,500 over budget, mainly because of additional data-cleanup work. Staff training is in progress, with a milestone date of November 3, 2026. The steering committee approved extending the pilot to Eastgate and Millbrook on September 9, 2026. [S1][S2]

The report identifies a risk that duplicate bibliographic records from the legacy system may delay go-live. Tomas Lindqvist, Data Lead, owns this risk, and a deduplication script is to be run by October 20, 2026. A second risk is that Larkspur’s lead migration engineer is leaving the vendor in November 2026; the project has requested a written staffing transition plan from Larkspur. [S3]

The listed action items are for Elena Vasquez to circulate the revised staff training schedule by October 10, 2026; Tomas Lindqvist to deliver the deduplication report by October 20, 2026; and Finance to confirm contingency funding of $6,500 by October 31, 2026. [S3]

output.overview: Amendment No. 1 changes selected terms of the Master Services Agreement (MSA), effective July 1, 2026. It raises the monthly fee and availability commitment, lengthens the non-renewal notice period, and adds quarterly accessibility reporting. The amendment says all other MSA terms remain unchanged and that it prevails in case of conflict. [S1][S2][S3][S5][S6][S7]

findings.description: Both documents concern the agreement between Larkspur Data Services LLC as Provider and Harbor City Public Library as Client; the amendment identifies the MSA as dated March 1, 2025. [S1][S5]

The MSA sets the monthly service fee at $4,500.00 and states fees are fixed for the initial term, with fee changes requiring a written amendment signed by both parties. The amendment changes the fee to $5,200.00 effective July 1, 2026, to cover hosting and support of the digital archive module. The amendment is a signed written amendment and states that it prevails if it conflicts with the MSA. [S2][S5][S7]
The MSA requires written non-renewal notice at least sixty (60) days before the end of the then-current term; the amendment changes that period to ninety (90) days. [S1][S5]

The MSA requires monthly availability of at least 99.5%. The amendment raises the commitment to 99.9% and says the Section 5.2 service-credit mechanism applies to the new target. The MSA mechanism provides a credit of 5% of that month's service fee for each full 0.5 percentage point below the target, capped at 25% of the monthly fee. [S3][S5][S6]

The amendment adds a new Section 11 requiring Provider to deliver a quarterly accessibility audit report of the public catalog against WCAG 2.2 Level AA within fifteen (15) days after the end of each calendar quarter. No accessibility reporting obligation appears in the MSA provisions provided. [S3][S4][S6]

The amendment states that, except as amended, all MSA terms remain unchanged and in full force. Thus the MSA provisions provided on implementation fees, payment, support response times, backups, data protection, termination, and limitation of liability are not changed by the amendment's stated changes. [S2][S3][S4][S7]

The MSA signature block names Dana Whitfield for Provider and Marcus Oyelaran for Client, with both signatures dated February 20, 2025. The amendment names Dana Whitfield for Provider and Priya Raman for Client, with both signatures dated June 12, 2026. [S4][S7]

output.limitations: The comparison is limited to the supplied excerpts. The amendment changes the MSA's non-renewal notice period but does not specify a separate effective date for that change beyond stating that the Amendment is effective July 1, 2026. The excerpts do not provide further detail on how the revised service-credit mechanism is calculated against the new availability target.

output.overview: The documents agree on the approved budget and forecast overrun, but differ in spending-to-date figures because they report different dates. They also give different go-live dates and the finance memo raises an unresolved question about whether staff training costs are included in the forecast.

findings.description: Both documents state an approved budget of $180,000 and a forecast at completion of $186,500, an overrun of $6,500 [S2][S4].

The project status report gives spending to date as $112,400 as of September 30, 2026, while the finance memo gives $118,900 as of October 10, 2026. The figures are for different reporting dates, so this is a context difference rather than a direct contradiction [S2][S4].

The status report says the planned go-live date remains November 17, 2026, whereas the finance memo's schedule assumes go-live on December 1, 2026. The documents do not explain the differing dates or say whether the schedule assumption reflects a change, so the relationship is unclear [S1][S5].

The status report says Finance is to confirm contingency funding of $6,500 by October 31, 2026. The finance memo recommends that the steering committee approve $6,500 from the technology reserve; it does not state that the funding has been approved [S3][S4].

findings.topic: Staff training costs in the forecast
findings.description: The finance memo asks whether staff training costs of $7,800 are included in the forecast at completion. The status report notes staff training is in progress but does not state whether those costs are included [S2][S5].
The finance memo specifies a final implementation installment of $9,000.00 payable to Larkspur in December 2026. The status report does not mention this installment [S2][S5].

The status report provides operational detail: migration is 85% complete, with 412,000 of 485,000 records migrated, and identifies duplicate-record and vendor staffing risks. The finance memo does not address migration progress or those risks [S1][S3][S4][S5].

output.limitations: The finance memo gives a December 1, 2026 go-live assumption but does not explain whether it supersedes the status report's November 17, 2026 planned date. The documents do not resolve whether staff training costs are included in the forecast or whether the recommended contingency funding was approved.
